title: Interest rates move everything
desc: Why rates move stocks, and why the surprise matters most

cards.title: A surprise hike
cards.situation: Traders expected the central bank to hold rates at 4%. It raised them to 4.5%. What do stocks often do that day?

options.text: Rise: higher rates mean a strong economy
options.feedback: A strong economy helps, but a surprise hike makes loans dearer and cash more attractive. Stocks often fall on the day.

options.text: Fall: money just got costlier than expected
options.feedback: A surprise hike makes borrowing costlier and cash more attractive. Many investors pay less for stocks.

options.text: Nothing: rates only matter to banks
options.feedback: Rates reach everyone: loans, savings and what investors will pay for stocks. A surprise hike often hits stocks on the day.

cards.title: Rates: the price of money
cards.text: The **[[interest-rate|interest rate]]** set by the [[central-bank|central bank]] is the price of borrowing. When it rises, three things change.

cells.text: cost more for firms and home buyers
pays more, so stocks must compete
are worth less in today’s money

blocks.tip: That’s why stocks often fall when rates rise, and rise when rates fall.

cards.title: It’s the surprise that moves
cards.text: Markets price in what they expect. The move comes from the gap between expected and actual.

items.label: Expected versus actual rate decisions and how stocks often react

items.title: Rate day · no cut
items.label: Stocks drift flat, then fall 1.7% after the decision: no cut

cards.title: Cash fights back
cards.q: Your savings account paid 1% a year. After rate rises it pays 5%, with no stock risk. Why might some money leave stocks?

options.text: Cash pays well, with less risk
options.feedback: At 5% with no stock risk, safe cash now competes with stocks. Some investors move money across.
Companies don’t stop paying dividends because rates rose. What changed is that cash now pays more, with less risk.
Stocks can earn more over time, but with risk. At 5%, safe cash is a fair choice.
Nobody forces savers to sell. They choose to, because cash now pays well with less risk.

cards.title: Who feels it most?
cards.q: Rates rise. Why do fast-growing tech stocks often fall the most?

options.text: Much of their value rests on profits years away
options.feedback: Fast growers’ value rests on profits years away, and higher rates shrink what those far-off profits are worth today.
Fast growers usually pay small dividends or none. Their value rests on profits years away.

options.text: Higher rates cut their sales the same day
options.feedback: Sales don’t change overnight. Higher rates shrink what far-off profits are worth today, and fast growers rely on those most.

options.text: Tech companies can’t borrow at all
options.feedback: Tech companies can still borrow; it just costs more. The bigger hit is to what far-off profits are worth today.

cards.headline: You know why rates move markets.
lines: Higher rates make borrowing costlier and cash more attractive.
Stocks often fall when rates rise, and rise when they fall.
Markets move on the surprise, not the decision itself.
